- `near`, `far`: Clamping distances for ray segment intersection.
Initialize `count` as a zero tensor with shape `world_size`.
- If `irregular_shape` is true, split rays into chunks of 10,000.
- Otherwise, downsample rays by `downrate` along both spatial dimensions, flatten, and split into chunks of 10,000.
Create a `DenseGrid` named `ones` with size `world_size` and appropriate world bounds.
Compute ray direction normalization vector `vec`.
Replace zero components with $10^{-6}$ to avoid division by zero.
Calculate intersection parameters `rate_a` and `rate_b` for the bounding box corners relative to the ray origin.
Clamp $t_{min}$ and $t_{max}$ to the interval $[near, far]$.
Generate sample positions `interpx` along the ray segment between $t_{min}$ and $t_{max}$ using precomputed `rng` and `stepsize`.
Compute 3D coordinates `rays_pts` for all sample points.
Query the `ones` grid at `rays_pts` and call `backward()` to accumulate gradients, effectively marking the voxels traversed by the ray.
After processing all rays, increment the `count` grid where the gradient of the `ones` grid is greater than 1.
Time complexity is proportional to the number of rays and samples per ray.
Memory complexity is dominated by the `count` grid and the `ones` grid.
Performance depends on the number of training cameras and the resolution of the 3D grid.
Strengths include explicit visibility information.
Limitations include the computational cost of ray casting for large scenes.
It is used to initialize or refine geometry masks based on camera visibility.
